These pages contain lecture notes, examples, exercises, and supplementary
material for *Mathematics in the Modern World*.

::: {.callout-note title="Intended audience"}
The notes are written primarily for the BS Biology students whom I teach.
Whenever practicable, the discussion uses examples drawn from biology,
ecology, health, data analysis, and other situations that students may
encounter in their studies and subsequent work. The course also considers
less obvious applications: part of learning mathematics in the modern world
is recognising its presence in problems and decisions that may not initially
appear mathematical.
:::

## House rules

1. **Printed notes are available if you need them.** If you do not have
   reliable access to a laptop or mobile device, speak to me after class or
   during consultation hours. You do not need to explain your circumstances;
   I will provide the relevant printed notes free of charge.

2. **Attend regularly and arrive on time.** Much of our learning will happen
   through explanation, discussion, and guided work in class, and attendance
   contributes to the final mark under the syllabus and university policy.
   The notes are a guide rather than a transcript: our pace, examples, and
   order may change. Any change affecting examinable material will be announced
   clearly; you will not be assessed on an unannounced topic.

3. **Participate, ask questions, and seek help.** Questions are welcome in
   class, by email, and during consultation hours; longer or off-syllabus
   discussions are usually best saved for consultation. You will not be judged
   for finding something difficult. Ask classmates, compare notes, and come to
   me when something remains unclear—we are all part of your learning
   community.

4. **Expect biology to involve mathematics.** Population growth, inheritance,
   epidemics, ecological networks, experimental uncertainty, medical images,
   and protein structures all involve mathematical thinking. You will not be
   asked to train an artificial neural network; the goal is to recognise
   quantitative structure, interpret evidence, and reason carefully—skills
   useful in biology, medicine, everyday decisions, and many other settings.

   ::: {.callout-note title="A case in point: mathematics and biology"}
   My BSc Mathematics thesis used computational topology to turn structures in
   retinal photographs into numerical summaries and test their reliability
   under changes such as blur, rotation, and noise. It brings together
   mathematics, computation, and medical imaging. Curious readers can explore
   the [self-study TDA section](/computational-topology/) or the
   [project repository](https://github.com/reyjosephnieto/ph); the advanced
   mathematics is not required for this course.
   :::

5. **Be present and considerate.** I have no interest in teaching through
   fear, and questions are always welcome. In return, help maintain a
   respectful room: listen when someone is speaking and avoid side
   conversations. Keep electronic devices away unless I authorise their use or
   an accessibility need requires them. Giving one another our attention makes
   those *“Wow, talaga?”* moments much easier to reach.

6. **Bring a notebook and a pen.** Record definitions, ideas, examples, and
   questions in your own words rather than copying everything. After class,
   practise active recall: reconstruct the main ideas from memory, then check
   what you missed. Compare notes with classmates and ask me about gaps that
   remain.

   ::: {.callout-note title="Use of generative AI"}
   Generative-AI tools can provide another explanation, suggest practice
   questions, or offer a different perspective. Use them cautiously: they can
   sound convincing while being wrong, so check their claims against the notes
   and do the mathematics yourself. They cannot replace independent
   understanding and will not be available during graded assessments. Quizzes
   and recitations will be announced and completed in class.
   :::

7. **Work steadily, but keep marks in perspective.** Assessments will be
   proportionate to the available time and published criteria. I will identify
   enrichment as examinable or non-examinable, and examinations will not hide
   “curveball” topics whose status was unclear. You may still be asked to apply
   a familiar idea in a new setting. Focus on sustained effort and constructive
   use of feedback. Have faith in your ability—I do.

   ::: {.callout-note title="Language in our classroom"}
   The notes may mix British and American English; either is acceptable if your
   meaning is clear and consistent. Practising English will help with the
   biology literature, but it is not a barrier to participation. English,
   Tagalog, and Cebuano are welcome, as are questions in other languages when
   someone can help translate. If my accent or wording is difficult to follow,
   tell me—I can explain in Taglish whenever practicable.
   :::

8. **Read the notes before class.** I will aim to publish each set of notes at
   least two weeks before we cover it. You are not expected to master the
   material beforehand: skim the headings, notice the main ideas and examples,
   and bring any questions that arise. Mathematics can be difficult, but it
   becomes more approachable when studied steadily, explained patiently, and
   connected to meaningful problems.

9. **Correct mistakes—respectfully.** Address the idea, never embarrass the
   person. Please point out errors in the notes or in anything I say; a valid
   mathematical or factual correction may earn extra credit under criteria
   applied equally to everyone. Finding a mistake is not a challenge to my
   authority—it helps improve both the notes and the class, and I will be glad
   you raised it.
